**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better**

**To:** Engineering Leadership
**From:** Infrastructure Team
**Re:** Recommendation on AI hardware capacity for the next two quarters

**Summary**

We are approaching sustained saturation on our local inference and training hardware. The question in front of us is whether to purchase additional accelerators or to invest in raising utilisation of the fleet we already own. After looking at cost, latency, reliability, opportunity cost, and how easily we could undo either path, our recommendation is to spend the next quarter on utilisation work first, with a pre-approved budget trigger to buy hardware if that work does not get us enough headroom.

**Where we stand**

Our four A100-class nodes currently run at roughly 78% average utilisation during business hours, with nightly peaks that queue jobs for 20 to 40 minutes. That queuing is the real pain: it shows up as slower iteration for the research team, and it has started to distort behaviour, with people batching experiments less frequently and, in a couple of cases, quietly running work on their laptops rather than waiting. Meanwhile, off-peak utilisation drops below 30%, which tells us the constraint is scheduling and fragmentation rather than raw capacity. A meaningful fraction of GPU memory sits idle because jobs are packed conservatively to avoid out-of-memory failures, and several long-running training jobs monopolise nodes that could otherwise be shared.

**The case for buying**

Buying is simple and fast. Two additional nodes would cost approximately $180K including networking and support, and would immediately eliminate queuing. It would also give us a reliability margin we currently lack: today, a single node failure removes a quarter of our capacity, and we have no spare to absorb it. If our roadmap commitments for the customer-facing model refresh are firm, hardware is the lowest-risk way to protect those dates.

**The case for utilisation work**

But buying now would lock in decisions under uncertainty. The utilisation data suggests we own more capacity than we are using. Better job scheduling, memory-aware packing, fractional-GPU allocation for inference workloads, and a modest policy change reserving overnight windows for batch training could plausibly recover 25 to 30% of effective capacity — roughly the equivalent of one node — for perhaps six engineer-weeks of work we would mostly want to do anyway. Unlike hardware, that investment is almost fully reversible in the sense that it pays off regardless of what we buy later: a better-scheduled fleet is cheaper to operate whether it has four nodes or six.

There is also the opportunity cost to weigh. $180K is about a third of our annual tooling budget. Spent on hardware, it is gone; spent partly on engineering time and partly deferred, it preserves optionality. Hardware depreciates quickly in this market, and accelerator prices have been trending down as newer generations ship. Buying six months early means paying today's prices for capacity we may not need by year-end.

**Latency and reliability considerations**

The strongest argument against a utilisation-only path is latency. Scheduling improvements help throughput but do nothing for the interactive experience if peak demand keeps growing; a researcher waiting 40 minutes for a fine-tuning run will not wait 35. And squeezing more jobs onto shared nodes introduces contention risk — noisy neighbours, harder failure isolation, and more complex debugging. We should be honest that our reliability posture is thin either way: with four nodes and no spares, we are one hardware failure away from a bad week. If we do buy, we should consider one smaller, cheaper node explicitly designated as spare capacity rather than two full nodes.

**Recommendation**

Spend the next six to eight weeks on the utilisation programme, with a concrete target: peak queuing under 10 minutes and average utilisation above 85%. Pre-approve the hardware budget now so that if we miss the target, or if demand grows faster than forecast, we can order within days rather than restarting the discussion. This sequencing costs us a little time in the worst case and saves us a large capital outlay in the likely case.

**Uncertainty**

We do not know how fast inference demand will grow once the new product surface ships; our forecast has a wide error band in both directions. We also have limited experience with the scheduling tools we would deploy, so the 25–30% recovery estimate is informed rather than measured. Both risks argue for the staged approach: it keeps the decision reversible, and it converts a single large bet into a sequence of smaller, better-informed ones.

Happy to walk through the utilisation data in Thursday's infra review.

**MEMO**

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Working Group
**Re:** Buy vs. Optimise — Our Local Inference Capacity Decision
**Date:** Internal circulation only

---

We've reached the point where our local inference hardware is running hot. Queue times during peak hours have crept from seconds to minutes, on-call has been paged twice for GPU memory exhaustion, and the natural instinct in the room is to buy our way out. I want to argue, carefully, that we should not buy more hardware yet — that the highest-return move available to us is to improve utilisation of what we already own, and that buying now would likely lock us into a decision we can't easily undo.

Start with cost, because it's the easiest to misread. The sticker price of new accelerators is only the visible layer. Once we own them, we pay for power, cooling, rack space, and — more expensively — the engineering time to integrate, monitor, and maintain them. Our current fleet sits at roughly 30–35% average utilisation, which means for every three units of capacity we own, two sit idle. Buying more hardware at that utilisation rate is like adding lanes to a road nobody is driving on. If we can lift utilisation to 60–70% through better scheduling, batching, and model placement, we effectively double our fleet's capacity for the cost of a few engineering weeks. Even under generous assumptions about the price of our time, that trade is hard to beat.

Latency is the strongest argument on the other side, and I want to take it seriously. Right now, our tail latencies suffer because workloads collide: a batch job lands on the same node as an interactive request, and the interactive user waits. That is a real problem, and it's the problem people feel when they ask for more hardware. But it is fundamentally a scheduling problem, not a capacity problem. Dedicated partitions, priority queues, and smarter batching would address the collision directly. New hardware would only mask it — and mask it temporarily, because our workload is growing and the same collisions would reappear within a quarter or two, at which point we'd be having this conversation again with a larger fleet and the same bad habits.

Reliability cuts in the same direction. Our recent incidents weren't caused by insufficient aggregate capacity; they were caused by single points of contention — jobs pinned to specific nodes, no preemption, no graceful degradation. More hardware without better orchestration gives us more machines that fail in the same ways. Conversely, the work required to improve utilisation — queueing discipline, workload isolation, better observability — is precisely the work that makes the fleet more reliable. We get two benefits from one investment.

Then there is opportunity cost, which is the argument I find most decisive. The engineering capacity we'd spend procuring, racking, and integrating new hardware is capacity we would not spend on the product features our users actually notice. Hardware purchases also consume budget that could fund tooling with compounding returns: a proper scheduler, autoscaling for bursty workloads, or a caching layer that eliminates a meaningful fraction of requests entirely. Those investments keep paying. A GPU purchase pays once and depreciates.

Finally, reversibility. Buying hardware is a one-way door in practice. Once procured, it anchors our architecture, our power budget, and our procurement cycle for years, and reselling enterprise accelerators recovers a fraction of cost at best. The optimisation path is a revolving door: if we do the scheduling and batching work and find that utilisation genuinely cannot exceed, say, 50% because of hard workload constraints, we will have spent weeks and gained precise, defensible data about exactly what to buy and how much. That is a far better procurement case than the one we could write today, which rests largely on intuition during a period of peak-hour frustration.

I want to be honest about the uncertainty here. My utilisation figures come from coarse monitoring, and it's possible that a deeper look reveals our peak-hour demand is closer to saturation than the averages suggest. If that turns out to be true — if we find hard contention, not soft inefficiency — then buying becomes the right call, and we should buy without guilt. That is why I'm proposing a time-boxed effort: eight weeks of focused utilisation work with clear instrumentation, after which we revisit this decision with evidence rather than instinct.

**Recommendation:** Do not purchase additional hardware this quarter. Invest in utilisation: scheduling, batching, workload isolation, and measurement. Reassess in eight weeks with real data. If the data says we need capacity, we will buy it — and we will buy the right amount, with confidence that we're solving the problem we actually have.

I'm happy to walk through the numbers with anyone who wants to dig in.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering Leadership
**From:** Infrastructure Team
**Re:** Recommendation on our local AI hardware capacity

**Summary**

We are at capacity on our local GPU fleet during peak hours, and we must decide between purchasing additional hardware and improving utilisation of what we already own. After several weeks of measurement and analysis, our recommendation is to invest in utilisation improvements first, with a defined trigger to revisit hardware purchase in roughly two quarters if demand growth continues.

**The situation**

Our fleet of eight accelerators currently averages around 55% utilisation across the week, but that number hides the real problem: utilisation peaks above 90% during business hours and drops below 20% overnight and on weekends. The constraint is not total capacity but capacity at the moment people need it. This distinction matters enormously for the decision, because buying more hardware would add capacity across all hours, most of which we would not use, while better scheduling and workload shaping attacks the actual bottleneck directly.

**Cost considerations**

The capital cost of adding four more accelerators is roughly $180,000, plus an estimated $2,400 per month in additional power, cooling, and maintenance. That is a real and recurring commitment. By contrast, the utilisation work — a proper job queue, batch-size tuning, quantisation for our inference workloads, and shifting batch jobs like fine-tuning and evaluation runs to overnight windows — is mostly engineering time we would spend anyway, perhaps six to eight weeks of one engineer's focus. The opportunity cost of the hardware purchase is also worth naming: that $180,000 is roughly a year of an additional engineer, or the entire budget we have earmarked for the observability overhaul. Spending it on machines that sit idle 60% of the time is hard to defend while cheaper alternatives remain unexplored.

**Latency**

Latency is the strongest argument for buying hardware. Our interactive inference latency degrades noticeably during the afternoon peak, and queue times for on-demand jobs have crept from seconds to minutes. This affects developer experience and, for the customer-facing prototype, user perception. However, our measurements suggest that much of the peak-hour contention comes from batch workloads scheduled naively alongside interactive traffic. Moving those to off-peak windows, which the queueing work enables, should recover most of the interactive latency we have lost. We expect p95 interactive latency to improve by 30–40% from scheduling changes alone, though we should be honest that this is a projection, not a guarantee.

**Reliability**

Reliability cuts both ways. More hardware means more redundancy: today, a single accelerator failure removes 12.5% of our capacity, and during peak hours that is immediately painful. Better utilisation, by definition, means running closer to the edge, so any failure or unplanned maintenance has a larger relative impact. We think this risk is manageable — our failure rate over the past year has been low, and the queueing system we propose would include graceful degradation and priority preemption — but it is a genuine trade-off, not a free win. If our fleet were larger and our failure rate higher, the calculus would tilt toward redundancy through purchase.

**Reversibility**

This is perhaps the decisive factor. Utilisation improvements are highly reversible: if the queueing system proves too restrictive, we adjust it. If overnight batch windows stop working, we reschedule. Hardware, once purchased, is largely a sunk commitment — it depreciates, consumes power whether used or not, and reselling used accelerators recovers only a fraction of cost. Choosing the reversible option first preserves our ability to change course as we learn more about our actual demand curve, which is still evolving as our product direction settles.

**Recommendation**

We recommend the utilisation path: build the queue, reshape the workload schedule, and tune our inference stack, targeting 75% average utilisation and restored interactive latency within one quarter. We propose a clear decision point: if, after two quarters, peak-hour demand still exceeds capacity despite these improvements — or if a concrete project is blocked by hardware — we bring the purchase proposal back with better data on exactly what capacity we need and when. That future purchase decision will be far better informed than one made today.

**Uncertainty**

We acknowledge real uncertainty. Our demand forecast is based on three months of data and could be wrong in either direction; a new product initiative could spike demand faster than utilisation work can absorb. There is also execution risk: the queueing work depends on one engineer, and slippage there delays everything. Finally, hardware prices and accelerator generations shift quickly; deferring purchase carries some risk of paying more later, though historically this has been offset by falling prices per unit of capability.

We're happy to walk through the utilisation data in detail and to set the review checkpoint formally if leadership agrees with this direction.
